newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Australia Stock Exchange votes to demutualise.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Australia Stock Exchange votes to demutualise.

text.p: Members of the Australian Stock Exchange voted on Friday in favour of a plan to demutualise the exchange, clearing the way for it to be the first publicly listed stock exchange in the world.
At a special meeting convened by the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) in all of Australia's capital cities a total of 540 ASX memebers voted for the proposal and 22 against.
The "for" vote represented 96.1 percent of the total. A vote of 75 percent in favour was needed for the proposal to succeed.

"The vote means that ASX members have a clear view about the competitive pressures we face in global capital markets and the need to be structured appropriately to meet those challenges," ASX chairman, Maurice Newman in a statement.
Newman said the vote was a significant step in the move towards demutualisation but much work needed to be done to resolve a range of regulatory and supervision issues that arose from the decision.
"We have already commenced discussions with the Federal government and the Australian Securities Commission on these matters and are grateful for their co-operation," he said.

Under the demutualisation, the ASX plans to draft new articles of association while the membership rules would be overhauled to allow for a broader membership base that reflected other exchange users.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting in Sydney, ASX managing director Richard Humphry said apart from discussions with the government and the Australian Securities Commission (ASC), the ASX would also consult community groups affected by the Exchange's decision to demutualise.
"One of the issues that we see as a problem is the lack of understanding of the importance of financial markets and the role that the ASX plays in the market," Humphry said.
Newman said the ASX board's best guess at how long the whole process would take to complete was 12 to 15 months.
"It's our best guess, but many issues could arise," he said.
Newman said it was ASX's intention to establish the deepest and most liquid market possible for ASX shares.
"Anyone will be able to own a share. We feel that listing is the best way of promoting broad ownership," he said.
It is unclear what value would be attached to the shares included in the demutualisation, as they would only be issued after the Federal government sanctioned the process.

Humphry said it was futile to speculate on what value ASX members would receive from their shares but said if the ASX had listed on June 30, 1996, the approximate value would have been A$242,000 per member.
The ASX could be listed with independent supervision arrangements to be worked out with the ASC, Newman said.
"Such arrangements must be established with as much transparency as possible in order that the greatest integrity and potential liquidity can be achieved," Newman said.
The Australian Stock Exchange reported a surplus of A$19.39 million after tax and abnormal items in the year to June 30, 1996, up from A$14.65 million in 1994/95.
